newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian markets soar on tough budget hopes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian markets soar on tough budget hopes.

text.p: Italian financial markets soared to record highs on Thursday as international investors piled into bonds and the lira, betting on a tough budget in Italy's dash to join European monetary union.

Italian markets, which are highly volatile even in phases of political calm, displayed galloping optimism as the government put the final touches to its 1997 budget package -- an event which usually makes investors grimace.
"People saw Italy had been performing so well for so long," said Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.

"That, together with the recent German rate cut which signalled there is a strong will in Europe for EMU, meant people have decided to play it for all it's worth. They don't want to miss the boat," Jellinek said in London.

The lira held up staunchly against the mark, strengthening beyond the psychologically important 1,000 lire level to trade near a two-year peak at 995.25. Government bond (Btps) futures broke down barriers to forge a historic high.
The lira was quoted at 999.65 per mark by 1320 GMT while the December Btp future had tempered gains to stand at 120.35 from its record peak of 120.98 earlier.
Dealers said buying came from every direction, including U.S. and UK funds and Japanese investors. Optimism also prompted some talk of a possible interest rate cut soon.
Even the sluggish stock market rose more than one percent, although brokers said the gain was due to the lira and bonds.
Jellinek said he doubted anyone believed Italy would make EMU by its scheduled 1999 start, which means meeting Maastricht treaty criteria on budget deficit and debt levels by 1997.

"I think what they're discounting is that Italy will continue to push towards EMU and improve its fiscal situation and also that countries like Germany and institutions like the Bundesbank are working towards EMU," he said.

Bonds and the lira have risen steadily in recent days but the latest dash comes as the market awaits the unveiling on Friday of the first full-year budget produced by the centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
Speculation is rife about the size of the deficit-cutting measures in the 1997 package, which had been expected to be 32.4 trillion lire ($21 billion) of cuts and revenue increases.

Newspapers now say it could be a two-tranche affair totalling as much as 60 trillion lire. Analysts said the government may be playing a tactical game, hinting at a huge figure in order to win support for its real, more modest goal.

The government relies on support from the Communist Refoundation party to push through legislation in the lower house of parliament and the hard left has warned it will not accept cuts in pension and health spending.
Analysts say behind the Italian markets' strength is also investor faith that, ultimately, the far-left will not try to topple the government.
However one sceptical trader said: "There are lots of elements to worry about in Italy but for the moment nobody cares. They're taking the medium-long view, not the short one."
Francesco Giordano, senior economist at San Paolo bank in London, also sounded a note of caution.

"The government is probably going to come out with something which will surprise us with its strength. But at the moment it's unclear exactly what measures they will take and Communist support is by no means assured," he said.
